# Theoretical background and problem setting

Following the spirit of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview, I begin by formally
presenting the Reject Inference Problem in Credit Risk as understood and
approached in this thesis, so that the hypothesis formulation and the
theoretical properties of the proposed solution can be precisely formulated.
First and also following the approach of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview a detailed
description in natural language of the biasing mechanism in FIs is done, so
that each concept used can be defined properly avoiding confusions. Second a
measure theoretic characterization of the biasing process through its assumed
underlying random variables (RV) is given. Finally, a characterization of the available
data for the FI is done as observed realizations of this process and its random
variables. Although the main focus of this thesis is not bettering the formalization
approaches, I find it important to be thorough so that future work can properly
criticize this thesis.

## Concepts definition

When a financial institution (FI) is going to grant a credit, it has received
first some information related to an applicant. This information is constituted
by the features, which are then used in a scoring model ("model features") and
other characteristics e.g. whether the applicant dresses well in a face to face
application. Based on the received information the FI decides whether to approve
the loan. Almost always this decision will be dependent on a scorecard, which
based on some characteristics representable as numbers of the applicant returns
a score. These characteristics will be called "model features". On FI's approval
a financing contract can be concluded leading to disbursement.  A credit-agreement
after drawdown is termed "accepted".^[since the contract requires
the consent ("acceptance") of both parties] If an application does not lead to the
FI's payout, it is called "rejected".^[Note that no differentiation on whether rejection
came from the FI or the applicant is made]

If an accepted applicant fails to repay the loan on time or in full (as defined by the
FI), the loan is classified as a default (“bad” loan). Otherwise, it is classified as
a “good” loan. In line with this I refer to applicants as non-payers (bad) or payers
(good), depending on the eventual repayment outcome.

Whether an applicant turns out to be a payer or a non-payer is driven by their
individual circumstances^[e.g. income or health] and purely unpredictable events^[
like a bankruptcy out of a corruption scandal in the firm where the applicant is
employed or the applicant winning the lottery], which are termed "idiosyncratic shocks".
The individual circumstances can be seen as a set of characteristics containing the
model features and "hidden features".^[Note: hidden features contain both observed
features by the FI but not used in the score-card and unobservable ones] Ignoring
idiosyncratic shocks for a moment, one can think of the repayment outcome as being
determined *completely* by the applicant's full set of features. In this sense, being
a payer or non-payer can be viewed as an underlying property of the applicant, even
though it is not directly observable at the time of the decision. Consider that this
"fully deterministic form depending on the features" still does not imply that even
if the FI observed the hidden features and the idiosyncratic shocks, it could perfectly
predict the repayment outcome as it cannot know the exact dependence structure.

## Measure theoretic description

Let $X_m, X_h, Y, Y_m, Z, \epsilon$ and $\varepsilon$ be RVs on the
probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$. Define with 
$f_o, f_i \in \mathbb{N}$
$$
X_o: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(\mathbb{R}^{f_o}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{f_o}) \right), \quad
X_h: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(\mathbb{R}^{f_h}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{f_h}) \right)
$$

as the RVs generating the applicant's model and hidden features^[Note that even though
not all features are per se continuous and therefore naturally real numbers, a reasonable
assumption is that they are representable as real numbers]. The joint distribution of both
features sets is characterized by
$$
X : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(\mathbb{R}^{f}, \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f} \right) \right), f:=f_m + f_h
$$
with
$$
\forall \omega \in \Omega: X(\omega) := \begin{pmatrix} X_m(\omega) \\ X_h(\omega) \end{pmatrix}
$$
Further with $V$ a placeholder for $Y, Z$ and $Y_m$ let
$$
V : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left( E_V, 2^{E_V} \right)
$$
with
$$
E_Y = \{g,b\}, \quad E_Z = \{a,r\}, \quad E_{Y_m} = \{g,b, \texttt{na}\}
$$

be the RVs describing the repayment type, acceptance decision and observable repayment
outcome of the loan applied for defined $\forall \omega \in \Omega$ as
$$
Y(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    b & \text{if applicant is a defaulter} \\
    g & \text{if applicant is a payer}
\end{cases} ,
$$
$$
Z(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    a & \text{if applicant gets accepted (financed)} \\
    r & \text{if applicant gets rejected (non-financed)}
\end{cases}
$$
and
$$
Y_m(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    Y(\omega) & Z(\omega) = a \\
    \texttt{na} & Z(\omega) = r
\end{cases}
$$

$Z$ is more precisely modeled as a measurable function of both features sets. Let
$$
s : \mathbb{R}^{f_m} \to \mathbb{R}, \; 
\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f_m}\right)-\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}\right) \text{ measurable}
$$
be a score function and
$$
d : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{f_h} \to \{a, r\}, \;
    \left(\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}\right)
    \otimes
    \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f_m}\right)\right) - 2^{\{a, r\}}
    \text{ measurable}
$$

an acceptance decision function. Then

$$
\forall \omega \in \Omega: \:
Z(\omega) =
d\left(
    s\left(X_m(\omega)\right),
    X_h(\omega)
\right)
$$

Consider thereby that this form does not imply that $d$ "reacts" to every
component from $X_h$, i. e. a subsset of hidden features can (and realistically
will) be independent from $Z$. In this spirit, $Y$ can also be modeled as
$$
\forall \omega \in \Omega:
Y(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    \varepsilon(\omega) & \epsilon(\omega) = \text{external effect} \\
    \iota \left(X_m(\omega), X_h(\omega) \right) & \epsilon(\omega) = \text{no external effect}
\end{cases}
$$

with $\iota$ a 
$\left(\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R^{f_m}}\right) \otimes \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R^{f_h}} \right)\right)$
-$2^{E_Y}$ measurable function and
$$
\epsilon(\omega) : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(E_\epsilon, 2^{E_\epsilon} \right), \quad
\varepsilon(\omega) : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(E_Y, 2^{E_Y} \right)
$$

the RVs defining whether an external effect overrides the "usual behavior"
and what the external effect ends up causing (e. g. if there is a shock in the laboral
market and whether it is positive or negative for the applicant).
